questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which pattern most strongly suggests myasthenia gravis rather than Guillain–Barré syndrome?
choices: Rapidly progressive leg weakness with absent reflexes after infection
Stable weakness with sensory loss only
Fluctuating ptosis and chewing fatigue that worsen with use and improve after rest
Sudden unilateral facial droop with aphasia
questions.explanation: MG commonly causes fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness with usually preserved sensation and reflexes. The other patterns suggest different neurologic processes.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A client develops progressive bilateral leg weakness and diminished reflexes days after a gastrointestinal illness. What condition deserves urgent evaluation?
choices: Guillain–Barré syndrome with possible respiratory and autonomic progression
Only chronic osteoarthritis
An isolated eye-muscle disorder without airway risk
A problem that cannot affect blood pressure
questions.explanation: GBS often follows an infection and can progress from limb weakness to bulbar, respiratory, and autonomic involvement. Serial examination and respiratory assessment are needed.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A client with MG has a normal oxygen saturation but a weaker cough, trouble clearing secretions, and falling vital capacity. What is the priority?
choices: Wait for saturation to fall below normal before reassessment
Encourage a large oral meal
Treat pulse oximetry as proof of adequate respiratory muscle strength
Escalate for possible impending respiratory failure and prepare airway support
questions.explanation: Neuromuscular respiratory weakness can worsen before pulse oximetry becomes abnormal. Falling vital capacity and poor secretion clearance require urgent evaluation.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which bedside assessment best helps detect early respiratory decline in MG or GBS?
choices: A single pulse-oximetry reading without clinical examination
Serial ordered vital capacity or inspiratory-force measurements together with cough, speech, swallowing, and breathing trends
Only a routine temperature check
Ability to move one finger once
questions.explanation: Serial respiratory mechanics and bedside bulbar or breathing findings are more informative than oxygen saturation alone; trends guide timely escalation.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A patient with suspected GBS develops large blood-pressure swings, new bradycardia, and rapidly worsening weakness. What is the priority concern?
choices: Severe autonomic dysfunction plus possible respiratory compromise
Expected recovery after IV fluids
A harmless side effect of bed rest
Proof that neurologic monitoring can stop
questions.explanation: GBS may cause life-threatening dysautonomia and respiratory failure. Sudden vital-sign changes with progressive weakness need urgent monitoring and critical-care review.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which immune treatment plan is consistent with current guidance for appropriately selected significant GBS?
choices: Routine corticosteroids as the only disease-specific therapy
Automatic plasma exchange immediately followed by IVIG for every patient
Neurologist-selected IVIG or plasma exchange, with respiratory and autonomic monitoring
No immune treatment can help GBS
questions.explanation: IVIG and plasma exchange are established GBS options; routine corticosteroids and immediate sequential therapy are not recommended. Treatment choice depends on severity and timing.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A client with MG becomes unable to swallow safely during an exacerbation. Which action is appropriate?
choices: Crush all oral medicines and give with water immediately
Stop oral intake, protect the airway, and ask the team how to manage medicines and nutrition safely
Increase pyridostigmine independently until speech improves
Ignore secretions if oxygen saturation is normal
questions.explanation: Bulbar weakness increases aspiration and airway risk. Oral intake and medication routes require reassessment, and drug changes are directed by the neurologic team.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which treatment may be ordered for an impending myasthenic crisis in addition to early respiratory support?
choices: Only an unsupervised extra oral dose of pyridostigmine
Routine corticosteroids as a substitute for airway care
No neurologic consultation
IVIG or plasma exchange under specialist direction
questions.explanation: IVIG or plasma exchange can be used for severe MG exacerbation or crisis, but neither replaces airway protection, ventilation assessment, and trigger treatment.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which trend best suggests that neuromuscular respiratory support is working?
choices: Improving cough and swallowing, stable ventilation, and strengthening serial respiratory measures
A single normal pulse-oximetry number with a weaker cough
New inability to lie flat and increasing secretions
Worsening bradycardia and fluctuating blood pressure
questions.explanation: Improvement is judged by the patient's breathing mechanics, airway protection, strength, and hemodynamics over time, not one oxygen-saturation result.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: What longer-term need should be included in a GBS recovery plan after the acute phase?
choices: Assume full strength returns before discharge in every patient
Avoid discussing pain or fatigue because they cannot persist
Assess pain, mobility, skin and clot risk, swallowing, fatigue, and rehabilitation needs
Stop all therapies as soon as the patient can move a toe
questions.explanation: GBS recovery can be prolonged and involve pain, fatigue, weakness, and immobility complications. Multidisciplinary rehabilitation and individualized follow-up support safer recovery.
